title: More Words of Mine
text:
Forgive me,

literary friends,

my dear academic

friends, forgive me.

I did not follow the ‘career’ of a poet.

I merely grew up with this

vocation for gathering meadowlarks,

but I never knew how to tame them.

They are uncultivated, they do not bow.

They are wild,

they do not polish their violins.

They are plain,

they do not deck themselves in borrowed plumes.


So forgive them,

their uneducated song

is living and imperfect.

What can I do?

If I gather words of agony

I do not see whether they sound musical,

and if I find hopes,

I give them away,

however much they may lack

the exact measures.

Then,

leave me like this!

Leave me there, in the streets,

with them, the simple people.

Let Juan, María, and Pedro

repeat my songs,

carry them to market,

take them into the factories,

send them to the lumber camp.

Let them repeat them

now, and while

they need them.

Later, tomorrow, soon,

they will have forgotten them.

And that is all right.

So forgive me.

Forgive me

that in the midst of combat,

in the midst of prisons,

in the midst of beasts that torture,

in the midst of night and its ambush,

in the midst of victims and fear,

in the midst of filth and shame,

in the midst of gunpowder and fire,

in the midst of hunger and lamentation,

and in the midst of this dislocated world,

I sometimes lose the rhythm and do not count

on my fingers

each verse!

There is no remedy for that.

I do not know how to measure blood!

I do not know how to count tears!


I do not know how to rhyme weeping!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. Its direct address, colloquial register, and repeated protest against aesthetic measure are retained.

title: To All My Brothers and Sisters…
text:
To all my brothers and sisters

of the still-oppressed world.

Uniforms, machine guns,

courtyard, narrow corridors,

solid iron door,

black bolt and padlocks.

A mouth that opens

two yards by one and a half;

floors, ceilings, and walls

bare as the desert.

Tombs for the living

where specters crawl

whose only human thing

is the shape of the skeleton.

Even the walls seem

livelier and less dry!

Nowhere on earth are there

deeper pits

nor time that drags itself

along such motionless hands.

Nor can there be

a space so small

that hides so many pains,

that keeps so many secrets.

The corridors lie in wait

with hysterical lookout posts,

ambushes one can touch

like shackles of ice.

Five transistor radios

deafen the quiet air

so that the cries are not heard

in the night of torment.

Dark-backed racks

strike sparks from the wind,

but return beaten down,

their jaws hanging slack.

Either earth is very far away,

or heaven is very far away!

I do not know whether you know

what a prisoner then feels;

that climb of cold

from backbone to hair,

that trembling which slips

through the chinks of fear

and courage’s spur

blunted by powerless rage,

bound and helpless,

crucified in the stocks.

That ancient pain

that never had a cure,

of a cornered animal

struggling as a captive

at the mercy of those who use

cruelty as a right.

And to feel the soul filled with a hatred

that scrapes within!

They appear, like rats

from hell’s sewer,

before the man who has

no weapon but his silence.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The prison’s catalogued physical detail and the poem’s address to the oppressed are retained.

title: Ah, Carry My Heart to Heaven!
text:
Pilgrim angels who inhabit

the divine dwellings of the East

and, rocked upon the bright air,

wander through mortal spaces.


To you a loving soul

begs unceasingly in her lament

for wings, to cross the firmament’s

blue path of air.


Cover me with the fearful mist

that blinds mortals in the night,

and in your pure fraternal arms

carry me there where my beloved rests.


Lead me to the sun where rests,

beneath a canopy of gleaming gold,

the beloved for whom I weep so much,

the genius of the passion that torments me.


Ah! Carry my heart to heaven,

and if afterward you choose to punish me,

tear me apart in the air, and I bless

your mercy and my blissful flight.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original; the elevated apostrophe and five enclosed stanzas are preserved.

title: Nothing Is Sadder Than the Last Farewell
text:
If two have loved each other with their souls in life

and at last in life the two part,

Do you know that grief felt is so great

that nothing is sadder than the last farewell!


In that word they briefly murmur,

in that groan both breathe out,

they promise neither to meet nor swear love,

for in that word they say farewell!


There is no complaint deeper, no sigh longer

than that word the two say:

the soul yields to horrible lethargy;

life ends in saying farewell!


At last death has entered life,

and at last for both of us we both die;

at last the appointed hour has come,

the saddest hour… the last farewell!


Never again in life, gentle companion,

never again shall the two of us see each other;

therefore my last utterance is so sad,

that nothing is sadder than the last farewell!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. Refrain, exclamation, and end-rhyme-oriented quatrain structure are retained.

title: To Isabella the Catholic
text:
If eyes could attain

to discover the immense sorrow

of the red stars,

on heaven’s summit

they would find you among the holy multitude.


You, alone, lend to the heavens, brighter than the sun, your halo:

gold transformed into the splendid corolla

which struck terror in the Moor.


O land governed

by your sacred and victorious scepter,

as it saw itself raised high!

O fortunate people,

O glorious throne of Iberia!


For you that noble endeavor

crowned the Christian people with fame;

for you, master of the sea,

the sovereign genius

found a new world in the Ocean.


But to your soul

two worlds on earth were narrow space,

and toward a third palm

to conquer by right

your spirit rose still farther.


Queen and saint alike,

from majesty to majesty you rose,

and reached where

the sun itself rises,

and seated yourself above the stars.


O sacred one! O great matron

of the Christian flock! O my queen!

Be for the crown

you once sustained

an invincible shelter and pious guardian.


Bless and encourage

the adored, childlike, pure head

that wears your diadem today,

and beneath the tenderness

of your divine love may it grow secure.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The royal-Catholic rhetoric and historical claims are retained as the speaker’s address.

title: Liberty
text:
The young men are smiling,

the old men are rejoicing

because, companions, they say

there is liberty for the people.


The throng is all song,

the bell towers, clamor,

the balconies, lights,

and the little squares, festivities.


A great novelty in the laws,

which, I swear, I do not understand,

happens when we see men

in such jubilation.


Many blessings, the learned say,

are preparing for the kingdom;

if men gain by it,

I rejoice for the men;


But for us women,

I neither praise it nor feel it,

for though laws may change

there are no rights for us.


Liberty! What does it matter to us?

What do we gain, what shall we have?

A prison as a tribune

and a needle as a right?


Liberty! What use is it to us

if our tyrants are

not the yoke of monarchs,

but the yoke of our sex?


Liberty! Is it not a bloody

sarcasm they make of us

by repeating that cry

before our irons?


Liberty! Ah, for weeping

we had it in every age;

with despots we wept,

with taxes we shall weep;


For these men, humane

and generous, like those others,

are ready in every century

to sanction our pains.


The young men are proud,

the old men are rejoicing,

equality is in the homeland,

liberty in the kingdom.


But I tell you, companions,

that the law is theirs alone,

that women are not counted

nor is there a Nation for this sex.


Therefore, though I hear them,

I neither applaud nor feel it;

if they lose, God repay them!

and if they win, good for them!
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. The 1846 date footer is omitted as bibliographic matter; the poem’s feminist irony and refrain remain.

title: Do Not Sing
text:
Do not sing, do not sing, for from far away come the shipwrecked,

come prisoners, one-eyed men, monks, orators,

suicides.

Doors come again, and the cold of stones,

of stairways,

and, in black clothing, those two ancient hands.

And a candle with a wavering smoky flame. And books. And

writings.

Do not sing, no. For it was the music of your

voice that was heard. I am recently dead, still

with tears.

Someone carelessly spat upon my eyelashes.

So I saw it was already late.


And I let the sun remain at my feet and the flies walk.

And a slow saliva slipped from my teeth.

Do not sing, for I have braided my hair, now,

and I stand before the mirror, and know well that I am fleeing.
editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish original. Portuguese original provenance is retained through the supplied Spanish version; its abrupt syntax and line breaks are preserved.

title: The Roosters Will Sing
text:
The roosters will sing when we die,

and a light breeze, with delicate hands,

will brush the edges, the

funereal silks.

And the sound of night will transpire

over the clear panes.

And crickets in the distance will break the silences,

the crystal stalks, cold, long, barren,

and the immense fragrance of the trees.

Ah, what sweet moon will see our calm

face calmer still than its great mirror

of silver!

What dense coolness in our hair,

free as fields at dawn!

In the mist of daybreak

the last star

rises pale.

What great stillness, without human speech,

without the lip of wolves’ faces,

without hate, without love, without anything!

Like dark lost prophets,

dogs in the countryside will barely converse.

Strong questions. Vast pauses.

We shall be in death

with that gentle outline

of a shell beneath the water.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of a Portuguese original; its contemplative, segmented verse is preserved.

title: Lineage
text:
The old beggars say nothing, do nothing.

They know it is useless and exhausting. They let themselves be. They let themselves be.

They let themselves be in sun or rain, with the same air of whole worth,

far from the body they leave anywhere.

They amuse themselves by stretching life through thought.

If someone speaks, his voice flees like a bird that falls.

And it is so unforeseen, unnecessary, and surprising

that to hear it properly perhaps they groan some ah.

Oh, they did not groan, no!… The old beggars are all Stoics.

They will place their misery beside the gardens of the happy world

but do not want those on the other side to know of the strange fate

that runs through them like a river through a country.

The old beggars live outside life: they have excluded themselves.

They open dreams and silences and naked spaces around them.

They have their empty kingdom, of high stars that do not shelter.

Their gaze never looks and their mouth neither calls nor laughs.

And their body neither suffers nor enjoys. And their hand neither takes nor begs.

And their heart is a thing that, if it existed, would suddenly forget.

Ah!, the old beggars are a people turning into stone.

That people, which is mine.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of a Portuguese original. The stark repetitions and final identification are retained.

title: Letter
text:
I, yes—but what of the evening star, rising and descending

from the heavens, weary and forgotten?

And the poor, who knocked at doors, to no avail, making

night and day tremble with their dry fists?

And the children, crying with terrified hearts: ‘why

does no one answer us?’

And the roads, and the empty roads, with their hands stretched

out uselessly?

And the motionless saint, who lets things go on their way?

And the musics shut in boxes, sighing with wings

folded?


Ah!—I, yes—because I have already wept everything, and dismissed my

used, sad body,

and my tears washed it, and night’s silence dried it.

But the dead, who buried dreamed of light

doves and bright flowers,

and those in mid-sea who thought of the message the shore

would swiftly unroll to their fingers…

But those who fell asleep from too much vigil—and whom I

do not know whether they will wake…

and those who died of waiting too long…—and whom I do not know were saved.


I, yes. But all this, all these eyes fixed on you, high

in life,

I do not know whether they will look at you as I do,

reborn and stripped of vengeance,

the day you need forgiveness.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of a Portuguese original. The broken interrogative syntax and final conditional are preserved.

title: The Dead Horse
text:
I saw the dawn mist

slide its silver gestures,

move an opaline density

in that portico of dream.


At the border there was a dead horse.


Crystal grains rolled over

its clear flank: and some wind

made its mane, small,

an arabesque, a sad adornment


—and moved the dead horse’s tail.


The stars still lived

and had not yet been born

ah! the flowers of that day…


—but its body was a bed:


a garden of lilies, the dead horse.


Many travelers contemplated

the fluid music, the dew-covered

great emerald flies

arriving in a murmurous stream.


Ahead, sad, the dead horse.


And living horses were seen,

tall as slender ships,

galloping in the fine air,

with happy profiles of dream.


White and green the dead horse was seen,


in the immense, destitute field

—and slowly the world turned

between its eyelashes, dim

in the moons of purple mirror.


The sun struck the dead horse’s teeth.


But everyone was in great haste,

and did not feel how earth

and the league’s course lacked

the agile, immense, ethereal breath

that was missing from that frame.


So heavy, the dead horse’s chest!
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of a Portuguese original. Capitalization and unusual syntax in the source are normalized only where needed for English grammar.

title: The Albatross
text:
For amusement, sailors sometimes
Hunt albatrosses, great birds of the sea,
Who follow, indolent companions of the voyage,
The ship gliding over bitter abysses.


Hardly have they cast them on the wet boards
When these kings of heaven, clumsy and ashamed,
Pitifully trail their wings,
Their great white wings like oars.


This winged traveler—how useless and how weak!
He, once so beautiful—how ugly and grotesque!
One burns his beak, sadistically, with a pipe,
Another mimics, limping, the crippled glider!


The Poet is like this lord of the cloud,
Who lives in the storm and laughs at the bowman.
Exiled on earth, suffering the jeers,
His giant wings prevent him from walking.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original; no external text was substituted.

title: Recollection
text:
Calm yourself, my grief, and make your anguish serene.

You longed for night. It is descending. Here it is.
A dark atmosphere covers Paris, bringing
peace to some and sorrow to many others.
While the crowd that yields to Pleasure,
its relentless executioner, roams the streets
hunting remorse beneath the wakeful feast,
you, grief, come to me. Give me your hand as you see
how it is possible to escape the already dead years
in their old garments upon heaven’s balcony.
Disillusionments now rise, as from the sea,
when the sun beneath an arch dies in the distance.
Now, like a shroud descending from the east.
Observe, my grief: the immense night advances.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version credited in the source to José Emilio Pacheco. The catalog title is blank; the English title is translated transparently from the explicit body heading ‘Recogimiento.’ A malformed soft-hyphen sequence is silently normalized.

title: Cloudy Sky
text:
Your gaze seems veiled in vapor;

Your mysterious look—is it blue, gray, or green?—

By turns tender, cruel, dreamlike,

reflects the sky’s indolence and pallor.


You recall the white, warm, veiled days

that make captive souls dissolve in tears,

when, seized by a confused evil that strains them,

excited nerves mock the sleeper.


At times you resemble those lovely landscapes

that suns of misty seasons light…

And how you shine, O wet landscape

through which rays pass amid a veil of fog!


O dangerous woman, O seductive climates!

Shall I end by worshiping your snows and frosts,

and at last draw from implacable winter

pleasures sharper than ice and the sword?
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original; the sustained address and questions remain.

title: Spleen
text:
I am like that king of a rainy country,
rich yet powerless, young though infirm,
who, scorning the compliments of his hundred counselors,
grows bored with his dogs and other animals.
Nothing can cheer him, neither hunting nor his falcon,
nor his people dying before the balcony.
The grotesque ballad of the favorite fool
does not distract this accursed invalid’s brow;
his blazoned bed turns into a crypt,
and the ladies, who find every prince pleasing,
no longer know what daring dress
will win a smile from the young skeleton.
The scholar who coins his gold has not been able
to draw the corrupted humor from his being,
and in the baths of blood the Romans made,
which old sovereigns often remember,
neither has he known how to revive such a corpse,
for instead of blood he has green Lethean water.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original.

title: Lethe
text:
Come to my breast, deaf and cruel soul,
Beloved tiger, monster of indolent air;
I want to bury my trembling fingers
In the thicket of your abundant mane;


To bury my aching head
In your lap full of perfume
And breathe, like a withered flower,
The night dew of my extinguished love.


I want to sleep! To sleep more than to live!
In a dream, sweet as death,
I shall press my kisses without rest
Upon your body polished like copper.


To drown my muffled sobs,
I need only your profound bed;
Powerful oblivion dwells between your lips
And Lethe flows from your kisses.


My fate, henceforth my delight,
Like a predestined man I shall follow;
An innocent condemned man, a docile martyr
Whose fervor increases in torment.


To drown my rancor, I shall drain
The nepenthe and beloved hemlock
From the delicious nipple crowning this breast
Which never held a heart.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original; the source footnote marker is omitted as bibliographic matter.

title: Elevation
text:
Above ponds, above valleys,
Above mountains and woods, seas and clouds,
Beyond suns, beyond ethers,
Beyond the boundary of starry spheres,


You move, my spirit, with all agility
And like a swimmer rapt in waves,
You joyfully furrow profound immensity
With unspeakable, virile delight.


Flee far from these morbid miasmas,
Rise to purify yourself in higher air
And drain, like a noble and divine liquor,
The clear light flooding limpid spaces.


Beyond weariness and deep griefs
That weigh upon misty life,
Happy is he who, with vigorous wings,
Can fling himself toward luminous, tranquil fields!


He whose thoughts, as if they were larks,
Lift their flight toward the morning sky—
He who soars above all, and effortlessly knows
The language of flowers and silent things!
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original.

title: Allegory
text:
She is a beautiful woman of splendid bearing,
Who lets her hair trail in wine.
The claws of love, the poisons of the brothel,
Slip over her granite skin without entering.

She mocks Death and Debauchery:
The monsters whose tearing, rough hand
Has always respected, in its fatal games,
The rude majesty of that proud body.

She walks like a goddess, reclines like a sultana;
A Mohammedan faith she puts in pleasure
And with open arms that set off her breasts,
With her gaze invites the mortal race.

She believes—or better, knows—this barren virgin,
Necessary nevertheless in the march of the world,
That physical beauty is a sublime gift
Able to obtain pardon for every infamy.

She knows neither Hell nor Purgatory,
And when the hour comes to enter Night,
She will look full at Death’s face,
Like a newborn—without hate or regret.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original.

title: The Sun
text:
Through the old neighborhood, where the shutters
Of little houses hide secret lusts
When the cruel star furiously strikes
City and fields, roofs and seedbeds,

I wish to practice my fantastic fencing,
Sniffing out in corners the chances of rhyme,
Stumbling over syllables as over paving stones,
Perhaps finding verses I dreamed long ago.

That nourishing father, who flees chloroses,
Wakes verses and roses in the fields;
Makes grief evaporate into ether
By filling brains and beehives with honey.

It is he who erases years for the man on crutches
And makes him festive like lovely girls,
And orders the grain to ripen and grow
In the immortal womb that longs to flower.

When, like a poet, he descends into cities,
He ennobles the lot of meanest things,
And enters like a king, without train or pomp,
Into royal houses and hospitals alike.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original.

title: Abel and Cain
text:
I


Race of Abel, eat and sleep;

God smiles upon you with pleasure.


Race of Cain, in the mud

fall and die miserably.


Race of Abel, your sacrifice

smells sweet to the Seraph!


Race of Cain, will your torment

ever have an end?


Race of Abel, see your crops

and your flocks prosper;


Race of Cain, your entrails

howl hungry like a dog.


Race of Abel, warm your belly

beside the patriarchal fire;


Race of Cain, in your den,

poor jackal, tremble with cold!


Race of Abel, love and multiply!

Your gold also breeds children;


Race of Cain, fiery heart,

beware those appetites.


Race of Abel, you grow and fatten

like a bedbug in wood!


Race of Cain, along the roads,

lead your fearful people.


II


Ah, race of Abel, your carrion

will fertilize the steaming soil!


Race of Cain, your task

has not yet been fulfilled;


Race of Abel, see your disgrace:

the pike has conquered iron!


Race of Cain, rise to heaven,

and throw God down to earth!
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire’s French original. Roman-numeral sections and the antiphonal pattern are retained.
